utterances.text: Let me just ask you, murders fall within the category of crimes against life and limb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next overview is the list of on-site investigations, completed investigations, and judgements delivered by courts for various categories. We see that the number of adjudications or, rather, judgements is lower because the total --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter seems to be reading the wrong list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a list of accused by category of person and type of crime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: If it is the list on page 65.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it on the ELMO a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed -- is it on the ELMO? 66.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 66. That -- on page 66 is the list of on-site investigations, completed investigations and judgements delivered by military courts in the army of Yugoslavia as of the 15th of May, 1999. It says "Military courts in the 1st Army's zone of responsibility," followed by military courts in the 1st Army command, et cetera. Air force and navy by strategic group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to intercede with a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The first list is a summary for all courts, and the one that is on the ELMO now gives the same overview but by courts, detailing information for all courts. The first one I mentioned was a summary for all courts. This one on the ELMO now is a breakdown. So we have the same totals, but they are broken down by courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But on page 66, we only have statistics for investigations, completed investigations, convictions, and acquittals. We don't see what it is really about. In the previous one that you commented upon, we see exactly what you are talking about. In view of the date, the date is the 15th of May, the courts have -- had been operating, as you described, since the 24th of March. That is for a little over 45 days. By some standards that you accepted in the operation of courts, was it the case that the number of convictions and judgements indicated a certain degree of efficiency; low degree, medium, high efficiency? What would be your assessment as a military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Just to say something about the scope of the work: 395 investigations were completed. 997 judgements divided into acquittals and convictions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading out this too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of the number of these courts, it is -- it can be qualified as a very high degree of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask: General, how was an investigation initiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigations would be initiated first of all by unit commanders. It was their duty. It was at the level of company commander. It was his duty to report accordingly if he found out that a crime -- that a violation was committed. Then there were investigation authorities, military police and others at the level of brigade and independent battalions. The main purpose of those units was to detect perpetrators of criminal offences and to collect evidence. They would be the ones who submitted reports to the military prosecutors. And the next level was the investigations judge of the military court. If he found grounds for an indictment, the military prosecutor would initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would initiate an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. If civilian organs find during an on-site investigation that it does not fall under their jurisdiction, they would refer it to the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out, could a civilian make a complaint directly to the military authorities, to your authorities, or must the civilian make the complaint to the civilian organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anybody could file a report. Any civilian, any man in the street who became aware of a violation or a criminal offence could report it to the competent authorities, and the prosecutor would be duty-bound to intervene. Any citizen had the right to submit either an oral or a written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a question out of curiosity: Mr. Nice, you have the B/C/S version of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is an address at the foot of the document which seems to be indicating the location of the document. Does this mean this document was taken from the electronic disclosure suite of the Prosecution? Could you tell me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll tell you later. While I'm on my feet, if we're looking at these documents for detail and if the Court looks at the English version of tables 2 and 3, it will probably at some stage need to draw to its attention that row 5 of table 3 is completely in error. It's a repeat of row 5 of table 2, and so you should simply strike out the figures in row 5 otherwise the maths don't work. And if you turn to the B/C/S version of table 3 in substitution for the figures 0, 22, 75, 35, 29, and 11, you should add figures 12, 175, 50, 47, 2, and 1. It's clear what's happened. The interpreter cast -- translator cast his or her eye briefly onto the wrong table when recording the details for table 3. As to the source of the document, I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you were indicating the address at the bottom of page 66. Is that right? It says here: "Documents of the legal department of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia." That's at the bottom of that page, if you were talking about page 66. You said there was an address at the bottom of the page. Then on page 67, it says: "47 documents of the legal department GSVJ," the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a location of common drive. We'll find out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich's view is that although the D reference is suggestive of it coming from a disk of some kind, she doesn't think it has any connection with the electronic suite. It's a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were documents of the legal department or administration of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. This is a review as of the 15th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I was asking you something with respect to efficiency, work efficiency. You said that efficiency was very high. I have in mind, of course, the short period of time, that is to say from the end of March to mid-May. That's just a little over a month and a half. And I'm looking at tables 1 and 2 in tab 14. So, General, I'd like you to comment that. For example, on the second table we see that crimes against life and limb, the accused there, incorporates killings. That column incorporates killings. And you have a total of 55 accused and 8 convicted. So would that then, for that period of time, be an indicator of high efficiency, medium, or low efficiency? High, average, or low?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the accusations and convictions, it is a high level, because an indictment has already been raised. Now, when it comes to convictions, that was slower. Eight cases or individuals were convicted, which means that not everything -- not all the data was collected. For example, on one day, the judges had 30 trials to deal with in Pristina, for example, the Pristina Corps, I mean. And on that particular day, only three trials went ahead, which means only three accused were brought in. So you can compare why the courts were not able to follow the tempo, the rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This will be the last question: Of what kind of killing would a soldier be tried and convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For any deprivation of life contrary to the law, whether through premeditated, unpremeditated, or whatever. Manslaughter, et cetera. If it can be proved, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has to be followed up but we don't have the time. We are now going to break for the day, General, and you will return tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. to continue with your evidence. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
